analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax owed on inherited fortunes.
analysis.headline: A Senate bill to repeal the estate tax, backed by 41 Republican senators including the Majority Leader, never received a committee vote and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would eliminate the federal estate tax, which is levied on very large inheritances when someone dies, and the related tax on transfers that skip a generation. It would keep a gift tax but cap its top rate at 35% and set a permanent $5 million lifetime exemption for gifts, adjusted for inflation. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: The heirs to the largest estates in the country. Only a small fraction of estates — those worth well over $5 million per person, roughly the top few tenths of a percent — owe any estate tax under current law, so the entire benefit of repeal would flow to the wealthiest families and to the very large estates that own farms and businesses worth more than the exemption.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the estate tax entirely for deaths occurring after enactment, and repeals the generation-skipping transfer tax, which applies when wealth is passed directly to grandchildren or later generations to avoid a layer of tax.

Keeps a gift tax but caps the top rate at 35% and makes permanent a $5 million lifetime gift exemption, adjusted for inflation, so large transfers during life would be taxed more lightly than under the existing 40% top rate.

analysis.who_pays: Everyone else. The estate tax raises tens of billions of dollars a year; repealing it would remove that revenue from the Treasury, meaning the burden would shift to borrowing or to other taxes paid by households that never come close to owing the estate tax.
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers who never owe the tax

drawbacks.text: Repeal eliminates a tax that under current law is paid only on the largest estates — estates below the exemption level (over $5 million per person, doubled for couples) pay nothing — so the entire revenue loss and the entire benefit concentrate at the very top of the wealth distribution.

The bill repeals the estate tax while keeping a lighter gift tax, decoupling the two: wealth could pass untaxed at death while lifetime transfers face at most a 35% rate with a separate $5 million exemption, a structure that invites shifting wealth into the least-taxed channel.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go almost entirely to heirs of the largest fortunes, while the cost — lost revenue of tens of billions per year — is spread across all taxpayers through higher deficits or other taxes. There is no meaningful benefit in the bill for households that would never owe the estate tax.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and no committee vote or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator John Thune introduced the bill on March 25, 2015, with 28 original Senate cosponsors named on introduction, including Majority Leader Mitch McConnell.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance, which was the only action it ever received in the Senate.
A total of 40 Republican senators cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The Finance Committee never scheduled the bill for consideration, and it never received a vote in the Senate or the House before the 114th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the estate tax survived, so general taxpayers kept the revenue it raises and heirs of large estates did not receive the cut. The strongest organized backers of repeal — the Senate Republican conference — did not get the change they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers generally; the estate tax survived

for.name: Sen. John Thune
for.role: U.S. Senator from South Dakota; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the estate tax repeal bill and assembled 40 Republican cosponsors.

for.role: Sponsor and cosponsors of the bill
for.what_they_did: Sponsored or cosponsored the bill; no Democrat joined.

for.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, though as leader he never brought it to the floor.

against.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee vote after it was referred to Finance; the bill took no further action.

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Opposed repealing the estate tax and supported keeping or raising it, signaling that any repeal reaching his desk would face a veto.

sides.party_line_note: All 41 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democratic senator signed on, and the bill never reached a vote on which a partisan roll call could be recorded.

industries.note: Repeal would eliminate the tax owed on inheritances above the roughly $5 million exemption, a benefit limited to the wealthiest few tenths of a percent of estates. The cost shows up as lost federal revenue borne by everyone else.
The estate tax is one of the few taxes aimed directly at concentrated wealth; repeal removes that revenue, shifting the burden onto other taxpayers or higher deficits.

Repeal of the estate tax would shrink demand for estate-tax avoidance planning, while the retained gift tax and its exemption rules would leave some planning work in place. The net effect on the industry is modest either way.
